tip: 'Boleh' = allowed, 'bisa' = able: 'boleh dipinjam' = may be borrowed, 'bisa diperpanjang' = can be extended.
'Asal' = as long as, provided that: 'asal pulang sebelum jam sepuluh malam' = as long as you're home before ten.
'Tidak boleh' = not allowed (spoken): 'tidak boleh merokok'. Signs say 'dilarang merokok'.
'Sudah boleh' = allowed now (was not before): 'sudah boleh pulang' = can finally go home.
House rules often use 'harus' + 'di-': 'sepatu harus dilepas' = shoes must be taken off.
'Tidak harus' = don't have to (optional), not forbidden. 'Must not' is 'tidak boleh'.
'Paling lambat', literally 'most late', means at the latest: 'paling lambat tanggal lima' = by the fifth. 'Paling cepat' = at the earliest.
'Sebaiknya' = you'd better / it's best to – advice, much softer than 'harus'.
'Sebaiknya jangan' = better not to – a gentle warning, friendlier than a flat 'jangan'.
'Sebaiknya' can follow the subject: 'kamu sebaiknya minta maaf' = you'd better apologize.
'Mesti' = 'harus' in relaxed speech – you'll hear it everywhere. In writing and formal talk, use 'harus'.
'Sempat' = managed to / had time to: 'masih sempat membeli' = still managed to buy.
'Tidak sempat' = didn't get the chance: 'tidak sempat sarapan' = no time for breakfast.
'Sempat' + activity = once did it for a while: 'sempat bekerja dua tahun di Makassar' = worked there at one point.
'Sanggup' = can manage it, heavier than 'bisa': 'tidak sanggup menghabiskan' = can't finish it.
'Tidak sanggup' + a cost = can't afford: 'tidak sanggup membayar sewa' = can't afford the rent.
The ending '-nya' can be 'it' after a verb: 'membawanya' = carry it.
'Tidak usah' = no need to (relaxed); 'jangan' = don't (warning): 'tidak usah bayar' is not 'jangan bayar'.
'Tidak usah repot-repot' = don't go to any trouble – the polite guest's phrase.
'Biar saya yang...' = let me be the one to: 'biar saya yang beres-beres' = let me tidy up.
'Tidak usah' works with 'di-' verbs too: 'tidak usah diganti' = doesn't need to be replaced.
'Silakan' = please, go ahead. In Java you'll often hear 'monggo' – same warm invitation.
'Mana saja' = any/whichever: 'loker mana saja' = any locker at all.
'Silakan' + 'di-' verb = extra polite invitation: 'silakan dicicipi' = please do have a taste.
'Wajib' = required – the word of rules and signs. In conversation people usually say 'harus'.
'Dilarang' = forbidden, the word on signs: 'dilarang berlari' = no running. Spoken: 'jangan lari'.
Normally people 'merasa' and things 'terasa': 'badan saya terasa lebih segar' = my body feels fresher.
'Itu-itu saja' = the same old thing: 'menu makan siang yang itu-itu saja' = the same old lunch menu.
'Tidak enak badan' = to feel unwell, literally 'body not nice'.
In speech, 'kalau' often replaces 'bahwa' after 'merasa': 'dia merasa kalau...' = he feels that...
